newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Sandvik posts mixed H1 with strong tool unit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sandvik posts mixed H1 with strong tool unit.

text.p: Swedish specialty toolmaker Sandvik AB on Tuesday posted a first half result in line with expectations but its performance paled in comparison with its Seco Tools unit which published results on Monday.
Sandvik posted an 18 percent fall in profit after financial items to 2.11 billion crowns for the six months against market expectations of 2.17 billion crowns.
"It was in line with expectations, maybe a bit on the low side, which reflected a different mix," CI Nordic Securities analyst Peter Karlsson told Reuters.
"But after Seco Tools posted better volumes than anticipated on Monday people started to expect more."

Seco Tools, which is one of Sandvik's seven business areas with a separate listing on the Stockholm bourse, on Monday posted a profit after financial items of 277 million crowns for the six months against 279 million a year ago.

The unit said sales increased by about 11 percent, with major markets such as Britain, France, Germany, the U.S. and Japan posting favourable increases, and the result for calendar 1997 would clearly be better than in 1996.
Seco's shares rose 11 crowns to 233 crowns on Tuesday while Sandvik's share closed at 261 crowns, 3.5 crowns above Monday's close but off its day high of 265 crowns.
Elsewhere sales were mixed and overall Sandvik's sales in the six months rose six percent to 15.48 billion crowns.
Sales in its unit Process Systems were low due to a low order intake in 1996 and Sandvik Steel sales were weaker in the U.S. in the second quarter and demand in Asia remained low.
Sandvik Rock tool's sales were high in mining markets but fell in certain markets in Europe and Asia.
Sandvik said overall order intake and sales rose considerably in the second quarter. Invoiced sales in the second quarter were the highest ever reported.
Sandvik said in a statement that the favourable sales trend would continue in the second half of 1997.
"A significant improvement in the business climate was noted in Europe during the second quarter," Sandvik said.

"However as a result of negative net financial items during the second half of the year, due mainly to share redemption, profit after financial items and expenses in 1997 is estimated to be largely unchanged compared with 1996."
Sandvik's share redemption programme carried out in June paid four billion crowns out to shareholders.

Analyst Angelica Hanson from Matteus said sales in North America in the second quarter were disappointing, only rising three percent against 10 percent in Sweden, 13 percent in Asia and Australia and 10 percent in Africa and the Middle East.
"But I think the second half will be better for Sandvik," Hanson said.

"Longterm we are positive on Sandvik, especially since it acquired Kanthal. I don't think we will see much share price movement as the share has gone well this summer and it just about acceptable at current levels."

Managing director Clas Ake Hedstrom told Reuters that he expected operating profit for 1997 to be about 500 million crowns higher than a year ago but lower financial items would mean an unchanged profit after financial items.
Sandvik posted 23 million crowns in financial net for the first half of this year against 230 million crowns a year ago.
Karlsson said Sandvik's longer hedging policy meant the benefits of the stronger dollar had not yet filtered through so the financial net was below expectations.
Sandvik said the weaker Swedish crown drove sales up about six percent in the first half.
"Currency movements will not affect earnings favourable until the third quarter since Sandvik continually hedges rates for exports from Sweden," the company said.
